keyVerseText: Which was the son of Melea, which was the son of Menan, which was the son of Mattatha, which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David,
rootMeaning: The name Ματταθά (Mattathá) is likely a shortened form of Ματταθίας (Mattathías), which itself corresponds to the Hebrew מַתַּתָּה (Mattithjah). This root suggests a personal name of Israelite origin, emphasizing heritage and identity within the people of God. The connection to Ματταθίας, which appears as the name of an Israelite and Christian, highlights a continuity of faith and lineage that transcends the Old and New Testament contexts, adding depth to its simple genealogical use.
usageInScripture: Mattathá appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in Luke 3:31, where it is used as a genealogical marker. The phrase 'which was the son of Mattatha' identifies a direct ancestor in the lineage of Jesus, underscoring the importance of tracing Jesus’ human ancestry. The consistency of the translation as a proper name signals its role as a historical and familial identifier rather than a theological term, yet it serves to root Jesus firmly within the covenant people of Israel.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Ματταθά as part of Jesus’ genealogy reminds believers that Christ’s incarnation is deeply rooted in the history and promises given to Israel. This name, linking Jesus to a faithful Israelite line, affirms the fulfillment of God’s covenant faithfulness through generations. It also points to the humanity of Christ, who shares in the lineage of real people with real histories. For the Christian faith, this underscores the reality of Jesus as the Messiah who comes from the people God chose, fulfilling the Old Testament hopes and securing salvation for all who believe.
keyVerseReflection: In Luke 3:31, the phrase 'which was the son of Mattatha' situates Jesus within a precise ancestral line, connecting Him to David through Nathan. The inclusion of Mattatha in this genealogy highlights the continuity of God’s redemptive plan across generations. This name, though briefly mentioned, anchors Jesus’ identity in the historical people of Israel, reinforcing that He is the promised descendant through whom God fulfills His covenant promises.
